Late_Blight shows dark brown necrosis — plants are dead/brown, not the green-wilt pattern seen in the test image.

## Summary of Analysis

**Test image features:**
- Whole plants severely wilted/collapsed
- Foliage remains green (no browning/necrosis)
- Multiple consecutive plants on black plastic mulch affected
- No visible leaf spots or lesions
- Sudden, dramatic collapse pattern

**Reference image comparison:**
- **Bacterial_Wilt** (best match): Reference shows plants completely collapsed while still green on black plastic mulch — nearly identical to the test image pattern
- **Southern_Bacterial_Wilt**: Similar but plants less dramatically collapsed; also shows more root damage focus
- **Verticillium_Wilt**: Gradual decline with V-shaped yellowing lesions — doesn't match
- **Bacterial_Canker_And_Wilt**: Plants turn brown/necrotic — doesn't match the green-collapse pattern
- **Phytophthora_Blight**: Fruit/stem lesions — doesn't match
- **Southern_Blight**: White mycelium at stem base — doesn't match
- **Gray_Mold**: Fruit/stem mold — doesn't match
- **Late_Blight**: Dark brown necrosis — doesn't match

The sudden, complete collapse of green plants growing on black plastic mulch — without any leaf spotting, yellowing, or necrosis — is the hallmark of Bacterial_Wilt (*Ralstonia solanacearum*), which blocks vascular tissue causing rapid whole-plant wilting.
